ideas.title: Reaction Rate Investigation
ideas.learningGap: Learners may treat rate as final product amount, change several variables at once, read any rising curve as an increasing rate or explain every factor as vaguely causing more collisions. They need a controlled experiment in which design choices generate inspectable time-series evidence and a weak control or mismatched collision explanation changes the next run.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences idea or deployed lab operates the complete C6.2 loop of factor choice, controlled mass/gas/endpoint measurement, repeated traces, graph interpretation and collision-theory explanation. The existing enzyme-condition idea is a biological assay with substrate, pH and denaturation state; it does not duplicate a general chemical-rate bench, and enzymes are not needed as a separate mode here.

ideas.title: Enzyme Activity and Specificity
ideas.learningGap: Learners may repeat lock-and-key language without distinguishing substrate, enzyme–substrate complex and product, assume every collision is effective, or read a temperature or pH curve without linking its rising and falling regions to different causes. They also need to distinguish a reversible low reaction rate under non-optimal conditions from irreversible active-site damage after denaturation and avoid treating one optimum as universal.
ideas.overlapCheck: The current co-ordinated-sciences catalogue contains B1–B4 ideas but no enzyme record. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no enzyme, catalase, active-site, substrate-specificity, enzyme-temperature, enzyme-pH or denaturation lab. The operated assay is therefore a genuine current gap.

ideas.title: Membrane Transport
ideas.learningGap: Learners may treat diffusion, osmosis and active transport as interchangeable movement labels, mistake random particle movement for net direction, describe active transport as diffusion in reverse without its energy requirement, or use turgid, flaccid and plasmolysed without connecting plant-cell state to water potential and membrane movement.
ideas.overlapCheck: The current co-ordinated-sciences catalogue contains B1 and B2 ideas only. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no diffusion, osmosis, active-transport, membrane or root-hair lab. Factors Affecting Diffusion Rate remains separate because it teaches controlled quantitative rate investigation rather than mechanism comparison.
ideas.revisedDirection: The Concord runtime could not be directly operated during the latest scouting pass, so this broad membrane candidate remains promising-needs-concept rather than build-now. Do not promote it until one narrower membrane relationship has an exact inspected cause, changing state and consequence.

ideas.title: Monohybrid Inheritance
ideas.learningGap: Learners may fill a Punnett square procedurally without distinguishing genotype from phenotype, homozygous from heterozygous or expected ratio from the noisy result of a small cross. A useful lab needs the learner to choose a cross, generate repeated synthetic offspring, and use a pedigree or test cross as evidence about an unknown genotype.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record operates a monohybrid cross, Punnett-square construction, pure-breeding test or pedigree inference. Reproductive-strategy and chromosome-division records are adjacent foundations but do not predict inheritance outcomes. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no Punnett-square, monohybrid, pedigree, genotype/phenotype or pure-breeding lab.

ideas.title: Homeostatic Feedback
ideas.learningGap: Learners may define homeostasis or list temperature responses without tracing a deviation from set point through control and effector action back toward the target range. They may also treat insulin and glucagon as interchangeable. They need to perturb a regulated variable, choose the opposing response, inspect a time trace and revise a response that drives the system farther from its set point.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record or deployed lab operates negative feedback, blood-glucose regulation or mammalian temperature control. B9 circulation and the reviewed B11 breathing response provide transport or control context but do not teach set points, insulin/glucagon/liver action or skin heat-loss state. The proposal remains distinct by making the regulated variable and error correction central.

In glucose mode, insulin or glucagon changes the liver-linked glucose trace in opposite directions. interaction.conceptualConclusion: Homeostasis maintains a constant internal environment through negative feedback around a set point. ideas.title: Food-Web Disturbance
ideas.learningGap: Learners may draw arrows between organisms without understanding that arrows represent energy transfer from food to consumer or that a web constrains ecosystem responses. They need to construct a valid network, classify each organism from its feeding evidence, then use the network to explain why one human intervention affects several linked populations and pathways.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record operates a food-web network through overharvesting or foreign-species introduction. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no deployed food-web, trophic-link, overharvesting or introduced-species lab. Trophic Energy Budget is adjacent but distinct: it follows transfer losses rather than changing network topology or node state.

interaction.conceptualConclusion: A broad, thin leaf and its named tissues form linked adaptations: carbon dioxide reaches mesophyll through stomata and air spaces, xylem supplies water, chlorophyll in chloroplasts transfers light energy, and phloem carries sucrose. ideas.title: Chromosome Number and Cell Division
ideas.learningGap: Learners may repeat chromosome, haploid, diploid, mitosis and meiosis definitions without tracking what changes before and after division. A useful lab needs a persistent chromosome state in which replication and the chosen division rule produce visible consequences for chromosome number and genetic identity, not a stage-ordering quiz.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record operates chromosome replication or division with visible diploid/haploid and identical/different outcomes. Reproductive-strategy and human-reproduction records use gamete concepts but do not teach the division state itself. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no chromosome-state, mitosis, meiosis, karyotype or ploidy lab.

ideas.title: Reproductive Strategies
ideas.learningGap: Learners may identify cloning and sexual reproduction but not use a population consequence to explain why genetic sameness can be efficient in stable conditions yet vulnerable to a changed environment, while sexual reproduction is slower/costlier but produces genetically different offspring. A useful lab needs a persistent population state and a bounded disturbance, not a two-column advantages quiz.
ideas.overlapCheck: The deployed Selection Pressure and Trait Frequency lab already owns population variation, environmental change, differential survival and generation-to-generation frequency change. A sexual-versus-asexual comparison could extend that system by changing how variation enters the population, but a separate disturbance simulator would duplicate its central learner relationship.

ideas.title: Alveolar Gas Exchange
ideas.learningGap: Learners may label the breathing system without linking the airway route, ventilation, capillary supply and exchange-surface features to oxygen and carbon-dioxide movement. They may also recite that expired air contains more carbon dioxide without producing or interpreting paired limewater evidence. They need one controlled system in which a surface or apparatus choice changes the gas trace and can be revised.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record or deployed lab operates human alveolar exchange, inspired/expired-air testing or the four human exchange-surface features. Photosynthesis Rate and Gas Exchange uses aquatic plants and net photosynthesis evidence, not alveoli or human air composition. The gap is genuine only while the route, interface and paired test share persistent causal state; a labelled diagram or indicator reveal would not be distinct enough.

interaction.learnerAction: Identify the named airway structures needed to complete an air-to-alveolus route, assemble the correct paired inspired/expired limewater flow, choose a control and alter one of ventilation, surface area, surface thickness or blood supply before collecting a qualitative gas trace.
interaction.visibleChange: One persistent system tracks the airway route, alveolus-capillary interface, inspired and expired oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour, plus the limewater result. Correct airflow through the paired apparatus makes the expired-air sample turn limewater cloudy sooner. A thin, large, ventilated and well-supplied surface maintains oxygen movement into blood and carbon-dioxide movement out; one altered feature changes the trace, while a missing control or reversed apparatus makes the conclusion uncertain.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The breathing system carries air to alveoli and associated capillaries. ideas.title: Blood Vessel Pressure and Exchange
ideas.learningGap: Learners may memorise artery, vein and capillary labels without connecting relative wall thickness, lumen diameter and valves to the pressure or function of each vessel. They may also say that capillaries exchange materials without linking their thin walls and proximity to cells to delivery and removal, or confuse whether named pulmonary vessels travel to or from the heart.
ideas.overlapCheck: The heart record uses vessels as circuit links but does not teach their structural trade-offs, qualitative pressure profile or capillary exchange. No current catalogue idea covers blood-vessel structure or exchange, and a read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no artery, vein, capillary, vessel-pressure, backflow or blood-exchange lab. The gap remains genuine only if fixed authentic vessel structures change flow and exchange evidence; arbitrary vessel construction or a three-image label exercise would be contrived.

interaction.learnerAction: Inspect fixed artery, capillary and vein cross-sections, place the correct segment in a simplified circulation path, send repeated pulses and use qualitative pressure, backflow and material-exchange evidence to diagnose one mismatched segment or failed vein valve. Route the named pulmonary and major heart vessels; in 0610 mode, include the additional renal branch.
interaction.visibleChange: A pressure trace is highest and pulsatile in the artery, falls across the capillary bed and is lower in the vein. An artery wall withstands the incoming pulse, an intact vein valve blocks reversal, and a thin capillary interface lets bounded materials reach or leave nearby cells. A wrong segment or valve failure leaves a visible pressure, backflow or exchange fault. The 0610 toggle adds renal artery and renal vein endpoints to the named-vessel map.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Artery, vein and capillary structures fit different pressures and functions: arteries have relatively thick walls and narrower lumens, veins have relatively thinner walls, wider lumens and valves, and capillary walls provide the short exchange interface. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it; the named pulmonary vessels are identified by direction rather than oxygenation.

ideas.title: Digestive Transit and Absorption
ideas.learningGap: Learners may memorise an organ diagram and enzyme table without linking sequence and state: physical digestion increases surface area without changing molecules; specific enzymes produce smaller soluble products; acid and bile create stated conditions; absorption follows only when suitable products reach the intestine; and unabsorbed residue proceeds to egestion.
ideas.overlapCheck: The current catalogue already contains Food Biomolecule Testing and Enzyme Activity and Specificity, but neither operates a bolus through named organs, secretions, changing pH, molecule state and absorption destinations. A coherent plant-station lab should let them choose an insect- or wind-pollinated design, run a pollination event, and then test safe germination conditions with visible seed/seedling consequences.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences idea operates flower-agent matching, pollen transfer, plant fertilisation or the three-condition germination investigation. Photosynthesis and plant-transport records are adjacent but do not cover reproduction. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no pollination, flower-adaptation, fertilisation or seed-germination lab.

ideas.title: Selective Breeding
ideas.learningGap: Learners may confuse artificial selection with environmental natural selection or treat selective breeding as a single choice. They need to operate the repeated human-selection, crossing and offspring-selection cycle across several generations, using observed offspring data to revise the next parent choice.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record operates selective breeding across generations, and a read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no deployed selective-breeding, crop-improvement or domestication lab. The existing inheritance record supports genotype reasoning but does not teach the repeated artificial-selection process. The gap is the human-directed breeding loop with visible population consequences.

ideas.title: Exercise Breathing Response
ideas.learningGap: Learners may report only that exercise makes breathing faster, collapse breathing rate and depth into one observation or omit the syllabus explanation linking increased blood carbon dioxide, brain detection and greater ventilation. They need time-series evidence across controlled demand and recovery, with a prediction that can fail and be revised.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record or deployed lab operates breathing rate, breath depth or carbon-dioxide-mediated ventilation. Heart Circulation and Exercise is adjacent because it measures pulse before and after activity, but its persistent state is heart flow, valves and circulation rather than respiratory control. This proposal remains distinct only if the learner measures both breathing variables and interprets their carbon-dioxide signal; a second exercise slider would duplicate the weaker surface pattern.

ideas.learningGap: Learners may recall the seven terms without applying their exact boundaries: externally caused motion can be mistaken for movement, simple enlargement for growth, breathing for respiration, and any discarded material for excretion. They also need to avoid treating one life-like observation as sufficient evidence for a sample.
ideas.overlapCheck: The co-ordinated-sciences catalogue contained no ideas at review time. A read-only search of D:/Cambridge Labs/cambridge-labs/app/labs.ts found no Biology or science lab and no experience teaching the characteristics of living organisms. ideas.title: Oxygen Debt Recovery
ideas.learningGap: Learners may use oxygen debt as a label for any post-exercise breathing, omit transport of lactic acid from muscle through blood to liver, or fail to explain why heart rate and breathing remain elevated after workload stops. They need to interpret a persistent metabolic recovery trace and see that both transport and oxygen supply are required within the specified syllabus model.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current record or deployed lab teaches lactic-acid accumulation, oxygen debt or liver clearance. Heart Circulation and Exercise already uses pulse and recovery evidence, while the B11 reviewed Exercise Breathing Response uses carbon-dioxide-mediated breathing rate/depth. This proposal is distinct only as the downstream metabolic layer: muscle/blood lactic-acid state, transport to liver and remaining debt. If implemented as another generic exercise graph, it should consolidate rather than become a separate lab.

interaction.visibleChange: The persistent surface tracks lactic acid in muscle and blood, transport to the liver, oxygen supplied by continued breathing and remaining debt. A missing transport or oxygen-supply link leaves the relevant state unresolved; completing both lets the syllabus recovery process reduce the debt.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Within the Cambridge syllabus model, vigorous exercise causes lactic acid to build up in muscles and blood and creates an oxygen debt. After exercise, continued fast heart rate transports lactic acid to the liver, continued deeper and faster breathing supplies oxygen, and aerobic respiration of lactic acid in the liver removes the debt.

ideas.distinctGap: The uncovered outcome is the metabolic persistence and removal of syllabus-defined oxygen debt; it is distinct from heart and breathing control only when lactic-acid transport and liver clearance remain the causal state.

assessment.summary: Curriculum importance 2: exact syllabus and book evidence establish the Cambridge oxygen-debt model. Concept strength 2: persistent compartments and route completion make continued recovery processes consequential and revisable. Authentic experimental potential 1: it visualises an authentic internal recovery mechanism rather than a practical. Resource quality 2: book, OpenStax and WJEC foundations collectively support the complete bounded sequence. Overlap risk 2: no deployed lab owns this mechanism. Need for interactivity 2: unresolved compartments explain why recovery persists beyond a static list. Tier judgment: build-now; rank 92 records later packet priority.

ideas.revisedDirection: Use one internal recovery surface: muscle → blood → liver, with continued circulation and breathing supplying transport and oxygen after workload stops. Let unresolved compartments expose a missing link. Avoid a data-collection simulator, calibrated kinetics, biochemistry beyond the syllabus and generic staged graph narration.

interaction.conceptualConclusion: A balanced diet requires the listed nutrient classes in suitable amounts and proportions, and food sources, importance and energy contribution are different kinds of evidence. ideas.title: Hormone Target Responses
ideas.learningGap: Learners may match glands to hormones without understanding that a gland-produced chemical is carried by blood yet changes only specific target organs, or may list adrenaline's effects without connecting them to one fight-or-flight signal. The current proposal identifies this gap but does not yet give most named hormone pairs consequential outcomes.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current co-ordinated-sciences record or deployed lab operates gland-to-blood-to-target hormone signalling or adrenaline's bounded effects. Homeostatic Feedback uses insulin and glucagon causally for glucose control, so this record must not duplicate that loop. Its remaining distinct content is hormone definition, gland identity, target specificity and adrenaline; novelty does not by itself establish lab need.

ideas.title: Stellar Life Cycles
ideas.learningGap: Learners may memorise one linear star sequence and miss that starting mass selects different giant stages and remnants or that supernova material can enter later star and planet formation.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current record or deployed lab covers protostar formation or mass-dependent stellar life cycles. The Solar System record treats the Sun only as a current stable star and does not duplicate this sequence.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Know that stable stars are formed as protostars from interstellar clouds of gas and dust due to gravitational attraction
Know that the nebula from a supernova may form new stars with orbiting planets

Know that the next stages of the life cycle of a star depend on its mass, limited to: (a) a small mass star (about the same mass as the Sun): red giant → white dwarf + planetary nebula (b) a large mass star: red supergiant → supernova → neutron star (c) a very large mass star: red supergiant → supernova → black hole

Describe the life cycle of a star: (a) a star is formed from interstellar clouds of gas and dust that contain hydrogen (b) a protostar is an interstellar cloud collapsing and increasing in temperature as a result of its internal gravitational attraction (c) a protostar becomes a stable star when the inward force of gravitational attraction is balanced by an outward force due to the high temperature in the centre of the star (d) all stars eventually run out of hydrogen as fuel for the nuclear reaction (e) most stars expand to form red giants and more massive stars expand to form red supergiants when most of the hydrogen in the centre of the star has been converted to helium (f) a red giant from a less massive star forms a planetary nebula with a white dwarf star at its centre (g) a red supergiant explodes as a supernova, forming a nebula containing hydrogen and new heavier elements, leaving behind a neutron star or a black hole at its centre (h) the nebula from a supernova may form new stars with orbiting planets
